groups.title: Two names for a street
groups.stimulus:
The municipal naming panel could not agree on a single date for the renaming of Lane Street. Local guides put it in 1931, when the council voted in favour of calling it Hester Lane. A trade directory used the name Hester Lane a year earlier, however. And it had not completely displaced Lane Street by 1935, when a greengrocer put both names on an invoice.

Whether any of these records settles the question depends on what counts as renaming. A council resolution standardises a name for public use. A directory helps a reader find a place, and its editor might prefer a name already widely understood. An invoice helps an order reach one address. When the greengrocer printed both names, this could have been a practical accommodation rather than a judgement about the merits of the name chosen by the council.

The panel eventually favoured printing both names on an interpretive plaque beside the contemporary street sign. It did not recommend that council records give both names equal status. A plaque aimed at explaining the history could show the uncertainty that an address used for delivering goods was meant to remove.

questions.stem: Which document shows Hester Lane in use before the council vote?
questions.explanation: The trade directory used Hester Lane in 1930, a year before the vote.

questions.stem: Why does the author list different purposes of resolutions, directories and invoices?
options: To explain how records can differ without any of them being wrong
To show that councils were required to seek the approval of directory editors
To establish which document first referred to Lane Street
To rank the records according to how widely they circulated
questions.explanation: Different records can accurately represent administrative, common and practical usage at different times.

questions.stem: Which statement describes the panel’s recommendation?
options: Change the official address back to Lane Street.
Treat both names as interchangeable in all council records.
Keep only Hester Lane on the new plaque.
Show both names on the historical plaque without establishing two official names.
questions.explanation: The historical display and the council records have different jobs; the panel did not recommend equal status in the latter.

questions.stem: What is the most cautious inference about the greengrocer?
options: The greengrocer may have wanted people familiar with either name to recognise the address.
The greengrocer found the new name in the directory.
The greengrocer was protesting against the change.
questions.explanation: The text suggests a practical accommodation without claiming to know the greengrocer’s motives.

groups.title: From the weather log
groups.stimulus:
The Halden observatory issued its first monthly weather bulletin in April. Before then, the observatory sent daily readings to the shipping office but did not publish them. The monthly bulletin reproduces the highest and lowest temperatures from the daily readings; it does not print the series in full.

An editor preparing the April bulletin noticed that the rain collector had overflowed on two days. She printed the rain total as “at least 61 mm” because those two catches had been entered as the collector’s maximum, not as measurements of the full amount. The thermometer readings were unaffected. The editor placed a certificate for the collector at the end of the bulletin, but did not say when a larger replacement would be installed.

questions.stem: Why did the bulletin use the words “at least”?
options: The two highest temperature readings were estimated.
The daily log omitted the first two days of April.
More rain fell than the full collector could register on two days.
The shipping office supplied a total from a different collector.
questions.explanation: Overflow means the recorded total includes only the collector’s capacity on those two days, so 61 mm is a lower bound.

questions.stem: The observatory published its daily readings before the first monthly bulletin.
questions.explanation: The passage distinguishes privately sending readings to the shipping office from publishing them.

questions.stem: Which question could a reader answer from the temperature figures described?
options: What was the lowest recorded temperature that month?
What was the temperature on each of the days when the collector overflowed?
What was the mean of the daily readings?
How often did the highest temperature occur?
questions.explanation: The monthly bulletin publishes the extremes but not the full series or their frequency.

questions.stem: The replacement collector will be installed before May’s bulletin is issued.
questions.explanation: No installation date is given.

groups.title: Evening rehearsal
groups.stimulus: A theatre group moved rehearsals to a school hall that could be rented at a lower hourly rate than its usual venue. The school stipulated that rooms must be left clear by nine, not that rehearsal merely had to stop at nine. At the first rehearsal the director ran a scene until the hour, leaving no time to stack chairs or lock cabinets. The group hired the caretaker to stay late, which cancelled out some of the rent saving. After that session it tested a plan allocating ten minutes for clearing. Cast members said the hall took longer to pack up when they used the collapsible stage, but little extra time when they worked on dialogue only. The producer split the timetable accordingly. She also set up a short handover with a teacher on evenings when equipment could be left in a locked storeroom. That arrangement was unavailable on Wednesdays because the storeroom held instruments for a class the next morning. Some members proposed hiring the original venue on Wednesdays. The producer asked them to compare total costs, including any transport for the stage, before making that decision. Her report said the school hire had potential savings but did not show that each rehearsal cost less. It recommended collecting more records after the timetable changed.

questions.stem: What caused the unexpected cost at the first school rehearsal?
options: The booked time ended without allowing for clearing the hall.
The school's rate rose at nine o'clock.
The cast forgot to book the teacher.
The stage was transported to the original venue.
questions.explanation: The group paid the caretaker after it used the whole slot for rehearsal.

questions.stem: The school allowed equipment in the storeroom on Wednesdays under the handover plan.
questions.explanation: The storeroom needed to hold instruments for a class.

questions.stem: Which comparison would best support a Wednesday venue choice?
options: The number of cast members who attended the very first rehearsal
Total costs of either option, including moving the stage if needed
The original rent per hour without other costs
questions.explanation: Hourly hire alone misses related expenses that differ between options.

questions.stem: After the producer split the timetable, no further caretaker fees were incurred.
questions.explanation: No subsequent fees are specified.

questions.stem: Should a train operator enable passengers to report inaccessible station lifts through its app? Select the strongest argument.
options: Yes; rapid reports can warn travellers in time to make an alternative plan, if alerts are verified and updated.
Yes; apps usually allow text entry.
No; online messages do not repair lifts by themselves.
questions.explanation: Timely verified information helps travellers manage a real barrier, even though it does not fix the lift.

questions.stem: All rooms on the top floor have a skylight. No room with a skylight is used as a darkroom. Some studios are on the top floor. Does each conclusion follow?
statements: Some studios are not used as darkrooms.
No top-floor room is used as a darkroom.
Some rooms with skylights are studios.
questions.explanation: 1. The top-floor studios have skylights. 2. The two rules exclude darkroom use. 3. Studios elsewhere are unspecified. 4. The top-floor studios supply examples. 5. No link establishes that.

questions.stem:
The allowed one-way walking connections are: Market → Bridge; Market → Garden; Market → Fountain; Bridge → Observatory; Garden → Lane; Fountain → Lane; Lane → Observatory; Station → Bridge.

A journey from the Market to the Observatory is still possible after the Bridge closes. Which extra closure would make that journey impossible?
questions.explanation: The Bridge closure leaves the Garden route and the Fountain route. Both must next pass through the Lane to reach the Observatory.

questions.stem: Eight of 17 bags contain a metal badge. Two different bags are picked uniformly. What is the chance at least one contains a badge?
questions.explanation: Subtract the chance of two failures: 1 − 9/17 × 8/16 = 25/34.

questions.stem: Of 36 badges, 14 have a triangle and 25 have a blue border. Every badge has at least one of those features. A badge with a triangle is selected at random. What is the probability it has no blue border?
questions.explanation: All 36 − 25 = 11 badges without borders must have triangles. The selection is from the 14 triangles, giving 11/14.

questions.stem: Should an exam venue publish a photo guide to accessible entrances? Select the strongest argument.
options: No; the guide cannot name every building in the area.
No; some visitors have previously used the building.
Yes; a current guide can reduce uncertainty for visitors who need to choose a step-free route in advance.
questions.explanation: The benefit follows from the stated guide and concerns the intended users.

questions.stem: The tool shed releases one key for each task. Keys are kept in separate boxes. No key in the yellow box is for digging. Every watering key is in the red box. One key is either for watering or digging, but is not in the red box. Which statement must be true?
options: It is in the yellow box.
It is for digging and is not in the yellow box.
Every digging key is outside the red box.
questions.explanation: Not being in the red box rules out watering. It must be for digging, which also puts it outside the yellow box. This says nothing about where other digging keys are kept.

questions.stem: A clerk must choose two separate files. A and B cannot be chosen together. C can only be chosen with A. D can only be chosen with B. Which pair is allowed?
questions.explanation: Only A with C satisfies both prerequisites and the separation between A and B.

questions.stem: Only A: 15; only B: 19; only C: 16; A and B only: 3; A and C only: 7; B and C only: 9; all three: 4; none: 11. How many people are in exactly two of the three groups?
questions.explanation: The relevant non-overlapping regions are AB, AC, BC: 3 + 7 + 9 = 19.

questions.stem: A clinic sends reminders to 90 of 150 patients. Eighteen reminded patients miss their appointment. Of all 150 patients, 42 miss their appointment. Which fraction of patients without a reminder missed?
questions.explanation: There are 42 − 18 = 24 misses among 60 unreminded patients; 24/60 = 2/5.

questions.stem: All demonstrations need a reservation. No reservation is accepted without an email address. Some staff training sessions are demonstrations. Does each conclusion follow?
statements: Some staff training sessions require an email address to book.
Every session requiring an email address is a demonstration.
No demonstration reservation can be accepted without an email address.
Some training sessions are not demonstrations.
questions.explanation: 1. The demonstration sessions require reservations. 2. Other bookings could need one. 3. The reservation policy applies to all demonstrations. 4. Only the demonstration training sessions are covered. 5. No such example is stated.

questions.stem: A game offers two independent chances to ring a bell. On each chance, Mia rings it with probability 1/3. If she rings it at least once she takes one token from a bag containing five silver and three gold tokens. What is the probability she takes a gold token?
questions.explanation: At least one ring has probability 1 − (2/3)² = 5/9. Then the token is gold with probability 3/8. Their product is 15/72 = 5/24.

groups.title: Shared workshop charging
groups.stimulus: The workshop uses energy credits. A machine in use consumes the stated number of credits each half-hour, and several machines may run at once. Time is billed by whole half-hours: for each machine separately, round any partial half-hour up.

questions.stem: How many credits are billed for 45 minutes on a lathe and 20 minutes on a drill?
questions.explanation: The lathe is billed for two half-hours and the drill for one, giving 2 × 8 + 5 = 21.

questions.stem: Four identical presses run for 40 minutes each. Their credits are split equally between three teams. How many credits does each team pay?
questions.explanation: Each press uses 2 × 6 = 12 credits. Four presses cost 48 credits, or 16 per team.

questions.stem: A team has 48 credits. After using a laser cutter for 1 hour and 5 minutes, what is the maximum time it could use a press?
questions.explanation: Three laser half-hours cost 36 credits, leaving 12, which buy exactly two press half-hours.

questions.stem: A member receives 25% off the total booked credits, rounded up to a whole credit after discount. What is the discounted bill for 30 minutes on each of the four machines?
questions.explanation: The bill before discount is 12 + 8 + 5 + 6 = 31. Pay 75% (23.25 credits), rounded up to 24.

groups.title: Music centre membership
groups.stimulus: The monthly fee applies to every current member. Fee concessions have already been reflected in the price. Overheads shown are for one month.

questions.stem: What is the combined monthly surplus from Strings and Brass?
Keys loses 25% of its members. How much is left after overheads that month if the fee is unchanged?
Calculate the mean monthly price per member across Strings and Percussion, to two decimal places.
questions.explanation: ((47 × 18) + (35 × 25)) ÷ (47 + 35) gives £20.99 to the stated precision.

questions.stem: If Percussion overhead rises by 20%, what percentage of fee income will then go on overheads at its existing membership? Give one decimal place.
questions.explanation: ((475 × 1.2) ÷ (35 × 25)) × 100 gives 65.1% to the stated precision.

groups.title: Post in three countries
groups.stimulus: An exchange office sells postage using quote units. The sender pays for the next weight band when a parcel exceeds one of the stated upper limits. The office adds a charge of 2 quote units to each tracked parcel after determining its ordinary price. One quote unit costs £1.60.

questions.stem: How much does it cost in pounds to send a tracked 500 g parcel to North?
questions.explanation: Exactly 500 g is in the middle band. North is five units plus two for tracking, so the cost is 7 × £1.60 = £11.20.

questions.stem: At which weights is ordinary postage to East cheaper than to both North and West?
options: Over 250 g and up to 500 g only
Over 500 g and up to 1,000 g only
questions.explanation: East has the lowest rate in the first band only; in the second and third bands another destination is cheaper.

questions.stem: A sender wants to post two untracked items to West. Each weighs 260 g. Sending them in one parcel adds 10 g of packaging in total; sending them separately adds 10 g per parcel. How much is saved in pounds by combining them?
questions.explanation: Separately, each 270 g parcel costs five units, 10 in total. One 530 g parcel costs seven units. The difference is 3 × £1.60 = £4.80.

questions.stem: If the price of the quote unit rises to £2.00 and charges in units stay the same, by what percentage does the price of a tracked parcel rise?
questions.explanation: All prices in pounds rise in the ratio 2.00/1.60 = 1.25, an increase of 25%.

groups.title: Finding a safe meeting point
groups.stimulus: Marin, a student on placement, is asked to show a visiting family to a meeting room. On the route they find a lift out of service. One family member says they cannot use the stairs; they are happy to wait on this floor if the team can meet them here. They have already waited thirty minutes, and Marin can contact the team’s coordinator.

questions.stem:
How important is the following consideration?

Whether an accessible room is free on the current floor and whether the team can meet there.
questions.explanation: This is central to arranging a safe and practical alternative without unnecessarily delaying the meeting.

questions.stem:
How appropriate is the following response?

Ask what would work for the family, contact the coordinator about moving the meeting and keep the family informed.
options: A very appropriate thing to do
A very inappropriate thing to do
questions.explanation: It involves the family, avoids an inaccessible route and gives the coordinator a chance to make a workable arrangement.

questions.stem:
How appropriate is the following response?

Ask the rest of the family to go upstairs and offer to explain the meeting to the person left downstairs afterwards.
options: A very appropriate thing to do
A very inappropriate thing to do
questions.explanation: It would let the meeting proceed, but excludes someone who wants to attend even though an accessible alternative can still be checked.

questions.stem:
How appropriate is the following response?

Stay with the family in the existing waiting area and ask reception for directions to another lift, without yet telling the meeting team.
options: A very appropriate thing to do
A very inappropriate thing to do
questions.explanation: Finding an accessible route is reasonable. Promptly updating the meeting team as well would reduce the chance of another avoidable wait.

groups.title: Two versions of a handover
groups.stimulus: A tutor asks Salem and another student to relay when a patient is due to return from a routine test. The other student says the return is at 14:00; Salem heard 14:30. The receiving team has asked for an update before making its plans. The staff member who arranged the transport can be contacted now. Neither student can see a record of the confirmed time.

questions.stem:
How appropriate is the following response?

Call the person who booked transport to verify the time, tell the receiving team it is being checked and relay the confirmed information.
options: A very appropriate thing to do
A very inappropriate thing to do
questions.explanation: This avoids transmitting a guess and gives the team a useful update while it waits.

questions.stem:
How appropriate is the following response?

Give the receiving team the earlier time as if it were confirmed, so it is ready either way.
options: A very appropriate thing to do
A very inappropriate thing to do
questions.explanation: The intention is precautionary, but presenting a guess as confirmed can disrupt planning when verification is available.

questions.stem: In this situation, select the most and least appropriate actions as a first response.
options: Verify the time with the person who arranged transport and then pass it on.
Tell the receiving team there are two unconfirmed times and ask them not to rely on either yet.
Pass on the time the other student quoted as confirmed so the receiving team has one clear answer.
questions.explanation: Verification directly resolves the disagreement. An explicitly provisional update is useful but incomplete. Reporting either recollection as confirmed is least appropriate.

questions.stem:
How appropriate is the following response?

Tell the tutor about the discrepancy and ask them to take over the call, even though Salem can contact the arranger directly.
options: A very appropriate thing to do
A very inappropriate thing to do
questions.explanation: Asking the tutor prevents the guess being reported as fact, but may add avoidable delay when Salem has a straightforward way to check.

groups.title: A different way to give feedback
groups.stimulus: At a student-run community event, Erin is collecting anonymous feedback. A visitor says they cannot use the online form and asks to give comments aloud. The organisers have approved a paper form that can be completed privately with help if the visitor wants it. The queue at the desk is long, and other visitors are close enough to hear a conversation.

questions.stem:
How appropriate is the following response?

Offer the approved paper form and the option of help in a quieter place, without assuming the visitor wants help.
options: A very appropriate thing to do
A very inappropriate thing to do
questions.explanation: It provides an accessible route while leaving the visitor in control of both assistance and privacy.

questions.stem:
How appropriate is the following response?

Take the feedback aloud at the desk immediately so the visitor does not have to join another queue.
options: A very appropriate thing to do
A very inappropriate thing to do
questions.explanation: This improves speed but overlooks an available private option when others can hear.

questions.stem:
How appropriate is the following response?

Point out the paper form and let the visitor decide whether to take it, without mentioning that help is available.
options: A very appropriate thing to do
A very inappropriate thing to do
questions.explanation: The paper form offers an alternative, but it may not be usable without the help the event can provide.

questions.stem:
How important is the following consideration?

Whether the visitor is comfortable with other people being able to hear their feedback.
questions.explanation: That matters to how a spoken option is offered; a quieter place is available and the visitor should be able to choose.
